Note on substitution: the reference chapter uses an annual “Singapore Residents by Planning Area/Subzone, Age Group, Sex and Type of Dwelling” release, which has since been retired from data.gov.sg’s catalogue (it no longer turns up under its old file name respopagesextod, or under a search for its own title). The nearest dataset still published at subzone level is the Census of Population 2020 table used here. It has a different shape to the retired series: it comes as one wide table with a single Number column that mixes planning-area subtotal rows (suffixed - Total) with subzone rows, rather than separate PA and SZ columns, so the wrangling below spells out the extra reshaping step that the original exercise didn’t need. It also reuses the Master Plan 2014 boundary from Part 01 rather than 2019, so both parts of this exercise share the same base map.

title: Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
4. Importing and Preparing the Data

4.1 Geospatial data
Re-importing the same Master Plan 2014 subzone boundary used in Part 01 — each exercise page runs as its own self-contained R session, so the object isn’t carried over automatically:

mpsz <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial/MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

Reading layer `MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL' from data source 
  `/Users/jedidiahasaf/Downloads/School/ISSS626/coursework-website/Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_Ex01/data/geospatial/MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson' 
  using driver `GeoJSON'
Simple feature collection with 323 features and 13 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6057 ymin: 1.158699 xmax: 104.0885 ymax: 1.470775
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84




4.2 Aspatial data

popdata <- read_csv("data/aspatial/respop2020.csv", na = "-")

The na = "-" argument matters here: SingStat suppresses small subzone counts with a literal -, and without telling read_csv() to treat that as a missing value, every numeric column in the table gets silently parsed as text.


4.3 Data wrangling
The Number column mixes two kinds of row: planning-area subtotals, named like "Ang Mo Kio - Total", and the individual subzone rows that follow each one. A forward-fill turns that into a proper PA column before the subtotal rows are dropped:

pop_sz <- popdata %>%
  filter(Number != "Total") %>%
  mutate(PA = if_else(str_detect(Number, "-\\s*Total$"),
                       str_remove(Number, "-\\s*Total$") %>% str_trim(),
                       NA_character_)) %>%
  fill(PA, .direction = "down") %>%
  filter(!str_detect(Number, "-\\s*Total$")) %>%
  rename(SZ = Number)







NoteData quality quirk



One planning-area subtotal row breaks the " - Total" pattern: Changi is written as "Changi- Total", with no space before the dash, while every other area uses "Changi Bay - Total" with a space. The regex above (-\s*Total$) allows for zero or more spaces so it still catches it — a plain " - Total$" match would have let "Changi- Total" slip through as if it were a subzone named "Changi- Total", similar in spirit to the YISHUN/Yishun case-mismatch flagged in the KNIME Data Analytics Lab exercise.


Computing the young / economically active / aged breakdown and the dependency ratio:

pop_sz <- pop_sz %>%
  mutate(
    YOUNG = Total_0_4 + Total_5_9 + Total_10_14 + Total_15_19 + Total_20_24,
    `ECONOMY ACTIVE` = Total_25_29 + Total_30_34 + Total_35_39 + Total_40_44 +
      Total_45_49 + Total_50_54 + Total_55_59 + Total_60_64,
    AGED = Total_65_69 + Total_70_74 + Total_75_79 + Total_80_84 + Total_85_89 +
      Total_90andOver,
    TOTAL = Total_Total,
    DEPENDENCY = (YOUNG + AGED) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`
  ) %>%
  select(PA, SZ, YOUNG, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, AGED, TOTAL, DEPENDENCY) %>%
  mutate(SZ = toupper(SZ), PA = toupper(PA)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(`ECONOMY ACTIVE`), `ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)

nrow(pop_sz)

[1] 224




4.4 Joining geospatial and aspatial data

mpsz_pop2020 <- left_join(mpsz, pop_sz, by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))
sum(!is.na(mpsz_pop2020$DEPENDENCY))

[1] 201


201 of 323 subzones get a dependency ratio. The rest (industrial estates, parks, water catchment areas, and a handful of 2014-vs-2020 subzone boundary renames) have no resident population in the 2020 Census and are left as NA rather than dropped, so the map below shows them un-shaded instead of silently disappearing.

5. Choropleth Mapping with tmap

5.1 A quick map with qtm()

tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(shp = mpsz_pop2020, fill = "DEPENDENCY")










5.2 A fuller map built from tmap’s elements

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Dependency ratio by planning subzone, Singapore") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits(
    "Source: Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (URA) and Census of Population 2020 (SingStat)",
    position = c("left", "bottom"))










5.3 Comparing classification methods
DIY: prepare choropleth maps using different classification methods and compare.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Quantile")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Equal interval")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Jenks natural breaks")








Quantile forces the same number of subzones into every bucket, which spreads colour evenly across the map regardless of how the underlying values are actually distributed — it’s the most visually “balanced” of the three but can group very different dependency ratios into one class if the data clusters tightly. Equal interval slices the value range into five equal-width bands; because most subzones sit in a fairly narrow band, that concentrates almost every subzone into one or two classes and leaves the rest of the legend almost empty. Jenks looks for natural gaps in the data itself, so the class breaks land where the dependency ratio actually jumps, which here sits closer to quantile than to equal interval.


5.4 Comparing number of classes
DIY: prepare choropleth maps using the same classification method but with 2, 6, 10, and 20 classes, and compare.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 2)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 2")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 6)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 6")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 10)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 10")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 20)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 20")








At n = 2 the map only distinguishes “below median” from “above median” dependency, which hides all the variation within each half. Pushing up to n = 10 or n = 20 starts creating classes so narrow that neighbouring subzones with almost identical ratios get visibly different colours, which reads as more precision than the data actually supports — with only 201 subzones, 20 quantile bins means roughly 10 subzones per class, each one a razor-thin slice of the value range. Something in the 5–6 range is where the map still shows a clear spatial pattern without either flattening the variation or manufacturing false precision.

title: Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
8. Reflections
The biggest difference from the reference chapter was upstream of any mapping code: the exact population dataset it names has been retired, so getting from “a CSV with an age/sex breakdown” to “one row per subzone with a dependency ratio” took real wrangling rather than a straight read-and-join. The Number column mixing planning-area subtotals with subzone rows, - used for suppressed counts, and the one inconsistent "Changi- Total" label were all things I only found by actually inspecting the output at each step rather than assuming the code from the reference chapter would apply unchanged. Once the join was right, the tmap classification and class-count comparisons were the part that most changed how I’d read a choropleth map going forward — the classification method and the number of classes are both editorial choices, not neutral defaults, and they can make the same underlying data look like a strong spatial pattern or a fairly flat one.

R spatstat G / F / K / L Monte Carlo
This is the second of the two Spatial Point Patterns Analysis readings for Hands-on Exercise 2: 2nd Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods. The first-order methods are in Part 01.

title: Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
1. Overview
First-order analysis asked how intensity varies across space. Second-order analysis asks a different question: do the events interact? Given the number of points present, are they closer together than chance would produce (attraction / clustering), further apart (inhibition / regularity), or indistinguishable from random?
Four distance-based functions answer this at a range of scales:








Function
Measures
Clustered when




G
distance from each event to its nearest event
curve rises above the CSR envelope


F
distance from random locations to the nearest event
curve falls below the CSR envelope


K
cumulative count of events within distance r
curve rises above the envelope


L
K, variance-stabilised to a flat zero line
curve rises above zero



Each is tested against a Monte Carlo envelope built from simulated CSR patterns. That envelope is the whole point: a raw G or K curve on its own tells me nothing, because almost every real pattern deviates somewhat from the theoretical CSR line.

                   quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

set.seed(1234)
childcare_ppp <- as.ppp(childcare_sf)

section: 5. A Note on the Hypotheses and the Number of Simulations
text:
5. A Note on the Hypotheses and the Number of Simulations
For every test below:
\(H_0\): the distribution of childcare centres in the study area is randomly distributed. \(H_1\): the distribution is not randomly distributed.
\(H_0\) is rejected at the 95% level if the observed curve leaves the envelope built from the simulated CSR patterns.
On nsim. The reference chapter uses nsim = 999. I use nsim = 99 throughout this page. With 99 simulations the envelope is the pointwise minimum and maximum of the simulations, which corresponds to a two-sided significance level of 2/(99+1) = 0.02 — comfortably inside the 0.05 I am testing at, and it keeps this page rendering in seconds rather than minutes, which matters because the site is rebuilt on every deploy. Where the observed curve leaves the envelope below it does so by a wide margin rather than grazing the edge, so the extra simulations would not change the reading. A marginal result would be a reason to raise nsim, and I would.

ImportantF and G point in opposite directions, and that is correct



G above the envelope and F below the envelope look like contradictory results but are the same finding stated twice: G is measured from events, F from empty space. A clustered pattern has short event-to-event distances (G up) and large voids between clusters (F down). If both pointed the same way, one of them would be wrong.
The computed table in section 10 confirms this holds in both study areas: G leaves its envelope upward, F leaves its envelope downward, and K and L leave theirs upward. Four statistics built on different distance definitions all reject CSR, consistently.
One caveat I want on the record. An earlier run of this page, before I fixed the seed, produced an F-function for Choa Chu Kang that never left its envelope at all — the opposite significance verdict from the one shown here. With only 74 points and 99 simulations, F in Choa Chu Kang is marginal enough that the answer moved with the simulation draw. G, K and L did not move. That is the concrete reason the seed is now fixed at the top of this page, and a warning against quoting a borderline Monte Carlo result as though it were stable. If this were assessed work with consequences I would raise nsim for F specifically rather than rely on a single draw.

title: Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
8. K-Function: Cumulative Counts
The K-function counts, for each event, how many other events fall within a distance r, averaged and scaled by intensity. Unlike G and F it uses all neighbour distances, not just the nearest, so it describes the pattern across a range of scales at once.

10. Where Each Curve Leaves Its Envelope
Reading significance off eight plots by eye is unreliable, so I compute it directly. For G, K and L a departure above the upper envelope indicates clustering; for F a departure below the lower envelope does.

crossing <- function(env, side) {
  d <- if (side == "above") env$r[env$obs > env$hi] else env$r[env$obs < env$lo]
  d <- d[!is.na(d)]
  if (length(d) == 0) "never leaves envelope"
  else paste0(round(min(d)), "-", round(max(d)), " m")
}

section: 11. What I Take From This Exercise
text:
11. What I Take From This Exercise
All four functions agree. In both Choa Chu Kang and Tampines, G, K and L rise above their envelopes and F falls below its own — four different statistics, built on different distance definitions, all rejecting complete spatial randomness in the same direction. Childcare centres in both towns are clustered.
The agreement is firmer in Tampines than in Choa Chu Kang. Tampines has 117 points to Choa Chu Kang’s 74, its curves leave the envelopes earlier and stay outside them longer, and its F result was stable across simulation draws where Choa Chu Kang’s was not.
Scale is the real finding. What matters is not that the curves leave the envelope but over what range, and the table in section 10 makes two things obvious. First, K departs over a far wider range than G in both areas — unsurprising, since K counts all neighbours rather than only the nearest, so it detects clustering that nearest-neighbour distances alone miss. Second, the two towns cluster at genuinely different scales: Tampines stays outside its K envelope well past a kilometre, while Choa Chu Kang returns inside it several hundred metres earlier. Those are two different spatial processes, and calling both simply “clustered” would throw the distinction away. A first-order KDE could not have told me any of this, because KDE has no notion of scale-dependent interaction.
What I got wrong, twice. First I read the F-function plot as contradicting the G-function plot and assumed I had mis-specified the edge correction. The two functions are supposed to point in opposite directions for a clustered pattern; writing out what each one measures from — events for G, empty space for F — fixed that.
The second mistake was the instructive one. I wrote up the significance verdicts from reading the plots, then built the table in section 10 to compute them properly, and the F result for Choa Chu Kang came out differently from what I had written. Chasing it down, the cause was not a coding error but an unfixed random seed: F in that area is close enough to its envelope that the verdict moved between simulation runs. Two lessons out of one bug — compute the crossing points rather than eyeballing them, and fix the seed before writing any sentence that depends on a Monte Carlo result.
Limitation, again. Every test here compares the observed pattern to complete spatial randomness within the planning area polygon. But a childcare centre cannot be sited in a canal, a cemetery, a reservoir or an expressway interchange, and a meaningful share of both study areas is exactly that. The CSR null is therefore slightly too generous, and some of the measured “clustering” is really just “buildings are where buildings can be”. The honest fix is an inhomogeneous null (Kinhom, Linhom) fitted to a population or land-use covariate rather than a homogeneous CSR, which is where I would take this next.
This is not a hypothetical worry. In Hands-on Exercise 3 I run the network-constrained equivalent of the K-function on Punggol, where the null only scatters simulated points along roads rather than anywhere inside the polygon — and the result flips from clustering to regularity. Some of what this page measures as clustering is the shape of the study area, not the behaviour of childcare operators.

1. Overview
Everything in Hands-on Exercise 2 assumed events could fall anywhere on a two-dimensional plane, and measured distance as the straight line between them. For childcare centres that assumption is wrong in a specific way: a centre sits on a street, a parent walks along streets, and two centres on opposite banks of Punggol Waterway are 80 metres apart in Euclidean terms and roughly a kilometre apart in walking terms.
Network constrained SPPA fixes that by confining both the events and the distance metric to the network itself. This exercise uses spNetwork to:

derive a network kernel density estimate (NKDE), and
perform network-constrained G- and K-function analysis.

The study area is Punggol.

text:
6. Network KDE Analysis

6.1 Preparing the Lixels
A kernel density estimate on a network is evaluated along the network, not over a grid. The first step is to cut the network into lixels — line pixels — of roughly equal length.

lixels <- lixelize_lines(network,
                         700,
                         mindist = 375)
nrow(lixels)

[1] 2645


The 700m target length with a 375m minimum means any leftover segment shorter than 375m is merged into the previous lixel rather than left as a stub. The count barely changes from the original 2,642 segments, which tells me most Punggol road segments were already shorter than 700m — this is a dense residential network, not a highway corridor.


6.2 Generating Line Centre Points

samples <- lines_center(lixels)
nrow(samples)

[1] 2645


These centre points are where the density will actually be evaluated. Note they are the centre of each lixel by line length, not the geometric centroid, so they always fall on the line even where it bends.


6.3 Performing NKDE

densities <- nkde(network,
                  events = childcare,
                  w = rep(1, nrow(childcare)),
                  samples = samples,
                  kernel_name = "quartic",
                  bw = 300,
                  div = "bw",
                  method = "simple",
                  digits = 1,
                  tol = 1,
                  grid_shape = c(1, 1),
                  max_depth = 8,
                  agg = 5,
                  sparse = TRUE,
                  verbose = FALSE)

A note on the arguments that actually change the answer:

kernel_name = "quartic" — the kernel shape. spNetwork also offers triangle, gaussian, tricube, cosine, epanechnikov and uniform.
bw = 300 — the bandwidth, in metres along the network. This is the single most consequential choice here.
method = "simple" — the simplest of the three NKDE variants. It treats network distance as a straight replacement for Euclidean distance in the kernel. It is fast and intuitive, but it is not a true density: the values do not integrate to the number of events, because mass is duplicated at every intersection. "discontinuous" and "continuous" correct that at increasing computational cost.

Attaching the computed densities and rescaling from events-per-metre to events-per-kilometre so the legend is readable:

samples$density <- densities
lixels$density  <- densities

samples$density <- samples$density * 1000
lixels$density  <- lixels$density * 1000

The high-density road segments are not a blob in the middle of Punggol. They are specific stretches — the roads threading the HDB precincts either side of Punggol Field and Punggol Central — while the roads along the waterway and the LRT viaduct run cold despite being geometrically close to plenty of centres. A planar KDE would smear density straight across the waterway and report a hotspot in the middle of the water, which is exactly the artefact this method exists to avoid.

7. Network Constrained G- and K-Function Analysis
The same complete spatial randomness question as Hands-on Exercise 2 Part 02, but with randomness defined on the network: the simulated points are scattered along the road network rather than across the plane.
\(H_0\): the observed spatial point events are uniformly distributed over the street network in Punggol. \(H_1\): the observed spatial point events are not uniformly distributed over the street network.
The test is at the 95% confidence interval, with the null rejected if the observed curve leaves the simulated envelope.

set.seed(1234)
kfun_childcare <- kfunctions(network,
                             childcare,
                             start = 0,
                             end = 1000,
                             step = 50,
                             width = 50,
                             nsim = 50,
                             resolution = 50,
                             verbose = FALSE,
                             conf_int = 0.05)

Reading the direction off the plots by eye is unreliable, so I compute where the observed curve actually leaves the simulated envelope:

rng <- function(d) {
  if (length(d) == 0) {
    "never leaves envelope"
  } else {
    paste0(min(d), "-", max(d), " m")

  Side = c("above upper (clustered)", "below lower (regular)",
           "above upper (clustered)", "below lower (regular)"),
  Range = c(rng(v$distances[v$obs_k > v$upper_k & v$distances > 0]),
            rng(v$distances[v$obs_k < v$lower_k]),
            rng(v$distances[v$obs_g > v$upper_g & v$distances > 0]),

ImportantConclusion of the test — and it is not what I expected



The observed curves leave the envelope on the lower side, not the upper one. Fewer centres fall within a few hundred network metres of each other than complete spatial randomness along the network would produce.
I reject the null hypothesis — the centres are not uniformly distributed along the network — but in the opposite direction to clustering. This is regularity (dispersion, inhibition). At longer distances the observed curve returns inside the envelope, so beyond that range the pattern is indistinguishable from random.
The seed is fixed above so these ranges are reproducible; without it the exact crossing distances shift on every rebuild.

title: Network Constrained Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
section: 8. What I Take From This Exercise
text:
8. What I Take From This Exercise
The result contradicts Exercise 2, and the contradiction is the whole lesson. Exercise 2 Part 02 concluded that childcare centres cluster at short range. Measured along the road network, the same kind of test on Punggol says the opposite: over the mid-range distances in the table above, centres are further apart than chance.
I do not think either result is wrong. They are answering different questions:

The planar K-function asks “are centres closer together than random points scattered over this polygon?” A large share of that polygon is water, park and reserve where nothing can be built, so the random comparison points are spread over space that real centres can never occupy. Against that null, anything confined to buildable land looks clustered.
The network K-function asks “are centres closer together than random points scattered over this road network?” That null already excludes the unbuildable space. What is left is the actual siting decision — and the actual siting decision turns out to space centres out, roughly one per residential precinct, which is exactly what a planner allocating childcare places by catchment would do.

So the planar “clustering” in Exercise 2 was substantially an artefact of the null, not a finding about childcare policy. That is an uncomfortable thing to discover about work I had already written up, and it is the strongest argument I have seen for why the network-constrained method exists.
Where the method is fragile. Three things would change the answer and none of them are statistical:

Bandwidth. 300m is a defensible walking distance, but it is a choice, and the hotspots move if I halve or double it. There is no bw.diggle equivalent here that picks it for me.
Network completeness. Punggol_St is a road network. Parents in Punggol walk through void decks, park connectors and the waterway bridges, none of which are in this layer. The network I am measuring distance on is not the network people use.
method = "simple". It duplicates kernel mass at intersections, and Punggol is full of intersections. The continuous method exists precisely to fix this and I would want to re-run with it before quoting any of these density values as real.

On nsim = 50. The chapter uses 50 simulations and I have kept that, but 50 is thin for a 95% envelope — it puts the pointwise significance level at 2/51, close enough to 0.04 that a marginal result would not survive scrutiny. Here the observed curve sits clearly outside the envelope across a contiguous band of distances rather than grazing it at a single point, so the conclusion holds. A single-band excursion would have been a reason to raise nsim rather than report it.
Connecting back. Reading Exercise 2 and this one together is the actual lesson. First-order KDE says where events are dense. Second-order G/F/K/L say whether events interact. Network-constrained versions say whether either conclusion survives once you stop pretending people travel in straight lines and stop pretending reservoirs are candidate sites. Each layer removed an assumption the previous one was quietly making — and unlike the first two steps, this one did not confirm the earlier answer. It reversed it. The thing I will carry forward is that in spatial statistics the null hypothesis is a modelling choice as consequential as the estimator, and a result is only as meaningful as the randomness it was compared against.

section: 6. Clark-Evans Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis
text:
6. Clark-Evans Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis
The Clark-Evans R statistic is the ratio of observed mean nearest-neighbour distance to the distance expected under complete spatial randomness (CSR).

R = 1 → random
R < 1 → clustered
R > 1 → regular / dispersed

\(H_0\): the distribution of childcare centres is randomly distributed. \(H_1\): the distribution is not randomly distributed. Confidence level 95%, so I reject \(H_0\) if p < 0.05.

6.1 Without CSR Simulation

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction = "none",
                clipregion = "sg_owin",
                alternative = c("clustered"),
                nsim = 99)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.50859, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)




6.2 With CSR Simulation
On the number of simulations. The reference chapter uses nsim = 999. Each simulation has to scatter 1,925 random points inside Singapore’s full multipolygon boundary, which is slow enough at 999 that it dominates the build time for this whole site. I use nsim = 99, which gives a pointwise two-sided level of 2/100 = 0.02, still well inside the 0.05 I am testing at. The observed R sits far outside the simulated range rather than near its edge, so the conclusion does not depend on the extra simulations.

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction = "none",
                clipregion = NULL,
                alternative = c("clustered"),
                method = "MonteCarlo",
                nsim = 99)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.50859, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)








ImportantConclusion of the test



R is well below 1 and p is far below 0.05 under both the analytical Z-test and the Monte Carlo version, so I reject the null hypothesis. Childcare centres in Singapore are clustered, not randomly distributed. The Monte Carlo version is the one I would quote, because it does not depend on the asymptotic normality assumption that the plain Z-test makes.

text:
7. Kernel Density Estimation
Clark-Evans tells me that the pattern is clustered. KDE tells me where.

7.1 Automatic Bandwidth Selection

kde_childcareSG_bw <- density(childcareSG_ppp,
                              sigma = bw.diggle,
                              edge = TRUE,
                              kernel = "gaussian")
plot(kde_childcareSG_bw, main = "KDE, bw.diggle bandwidth")








The bandwidth actually chosen:

bw <- bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp)
bw

   sigma 
312.3243 




7.2 Rescaling to Kilometres
The density values above are unreadable because the unit is metres — density comes out as “events per square metre”, which is a very small number. Rescaling the pattern to kilometres fixes the legend without changing the analysis.

childcareSG_ppp.km <- rescale.ppp(childcareSG_ppp, 1000, "km")

kde_childcareSG.bw <- density(childcareSG_ppp.km,
                              sigma = bw.diggle,
                              edge = TRUE,
                              kernel = "gaussian")
plot(kde_childcareSG.bw, main = "KDE rescaled to km")

NoteWhich bandwidth I would use



bw.CvL returns a much larger bandwidth and produces a smooth blob that says little beyond “the middle and east are busier”. bw.diggle and bw.ppl are far tighter and resolve individual towns. Baddeley’s advice is that bw.ppl is preferable when the pattern is a collection of tight clusters, and bw.diggle when the goal is detecting a single dominant cluster. Childcare centres are clearly the former — many town-sized clusters — so bw.ppl is the more defensible choice here, even though the chapter demonstrates bw.diggle first.




7.4 Comparing Kernel Functions

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp.km, sigma = bw.ppl, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"),     main = "Gaussian")

plot(density(childcareSG_ppp.km, sigma = bw.ppl, edge = TRUE, kernel = "disc"),         main = "Disc")







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

The four kernels are visually near-identical. That is the expected result — the choice of bandwidth dominates the choice of kernel, which is a useful thing to have seen rather than just read.

8. Fixed and Adaptive Bandwidth KDE

8.1 Fixed Bandwidth
A fixed 600m bandwidth (0.6 in km units):

kde_childcareSG_600 <- density(childcareSG_ppp.km,
                               sigma = 0.6,
                               edge = TRUE,
                               kernel = "gaussian")
plot(kde_childcareSG_600, main = "Fixed bandwidth, sigma = 600m")










8.2 Adaptive Bandwidth
Fixed bandwidth is a problem when the underlying point density varies a lot across the study area — which is exactly the case in Singapore, where the centre is dense and the west is sparse. Adaptive bandwidth varies the smoothing locally.

kde_childcareSG_adaptive <- adaptive.density(childcareSG_ppp.km, method = "kernel")
plot(kde_childcareSG_adaptive, main = "Adaptive bandwidth KDE")









par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(kde_childcareSG.bw, main = "Fixed bandwidth")
plot(kde_childcareSG_adaptive, main = "Adaptive bandwidth")







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))







NoteFixed vs adaptive



The adaptive surface keeps detail in the sparse western and northern areas that the fixed-bandwidth version smooths into near-nothing, while holding the dense central corridor together instead of fragmenting it. The trade-off is that the adaptive map is harder to explain to a non-technical reader, because the amount of smoothing is no longer constant across the map — two equally bright pixels do not necessarily mean the same thing.

section: 11. What I Take From This Exercise
text:
11. What I Take From This Exercise
The statistical answer. Childcare centres in Singapore are clustered at the national scale, decisively so — R = 0.51 with p effectively zero under Monte Carlo simulation. The high-density areas are the mature and newer HDB towns.
The methodological point that cost me the most time. The window matters as much as the points. Running Clark-Evans on the national pattern and running it on Choa Chu Kang are answering different questions, and the second is not a “zoomed-in” version of the first — changing the window changes the expected nearest-neighbour distance under CSR, which is the denominator of R. A pattern can be clustered nationally and close to random within a single town, and that is not a contradiction.
What I would flag as a limitation. The whole analysis treats Singapore’s land area as uniformly available for childcare centres, which is plainly false. Catchment reserves, airbases, port land and industrial estates cannot host a childcare centre at all. A clustering result measured against a CSR null that allows points anywhere on land will therefore always look clustered, partly for reasons that have nothing to do with childcare policy. A more honest null would restrict the window to residential-zoned land. That is beyond this exercise, but it is the first thing I would change.
Connecting to Part 02. First-order analysis stops at “where is it dense”. It cannot distinguish a pattern that is dense because the population is dense from a pattern that is dense because centres genuinely attract each other. The G, F, K and L functions in Part 02 are what separate those two.

text:
10. Reflections
The main friction point in this exercise wasn’t the sf workflow itself, it was that the reference chapter’s data sources have moved on: data.gov.sg no longer serves the Master Plan boundary, pre-school, or cycling path layers as Shapefile/KML, only GeoJSON. st_read() handles GeoJSON exactly the same way it handles a Shapefile or KML, so the substitution didn’t change anything downstream — the buffer, point-in- polygon, and density workflows all ran the same way once every layer was reprojected to EPSG:3414. The one thing worth double-checking whenever a dataset gets swapped like this is what coordinate system it actually arrives in — all three geospatial layers here came in as WGS84, whereas the reference chapter has some of them (the cycling path, in particular) already in SVY21.
